articles.sourceTitle: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
articles.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
articles.text:
Image Credits:Andrey Rudakov/Bloomberg / Getty Images

US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems

6:07 AM PDT · October 20, 2026

The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.

The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.

The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.

China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.

The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.

Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.

The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares.

The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.

In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Kate Park is a reporter at TechCrunch, with a focus on technology, startups and venture capital in Asia. She previously was a financial journalist at Mergermarket covering M&A, private equity and venture capital.

articles.sourceTitle: DeepSeek just open-sourced its inference engine
articles.title: deepseek-ai/DeepInfer: DeepInfer: High-performance, large-scale inference framework for DeepSeek models · GitHub
articles.text:
DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale.
Supported models:

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Supported features:

Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime
Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB
DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification
SWA bounded replay
Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler)
Batch-invariant inference
Deterministic sampling
Structured outputs

Feature details and configuration

Optimized kernels: FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, DeepSelect, and custom TileLang kernels.
DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification: accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1; DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE controls the maximum draft length (default: 5).
Decoder SWA bounded replay: reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length.
Asynchronous scheduling: overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default.
Batch-invariant inference: keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (NVIDIA only).
Deterministic sampling: produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 and pass a fixed seq_seed to SamplingParams (NVIDIA only).
Structured outputs: constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...} to SamplingParams; see examples.

Supported hardware:

NVIDIA SM100 GPUs
Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs

Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release):

A KV cache system
VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented)
Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode

Linux
GCC >= 13.0
Python 3.12
CUDA 13 (NVIDIA only)
CANN 9.2 (Ascend only)

Before building DeepInfer, please create and activate an empty Python 3.12 environment.
# Use `ascend` instead for the Ascend platform
# Keep it exported in the environment where you run DeepInfer
export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia
./build.sh

The default checkpoint, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, is
downloaded into the Hugging Face cache on the first run; set DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 to
run from a local copy instead.
python examples/offline_inference.py
See examples for details.

Measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode — each within one scale-up domain. To reproduce the benchmarks, see run_sweep.sh.

See eval/README.md.

DeepInfer is released under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE for details.

DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM, with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. We thank their developers.

@misc{deepinfer2026,
title = {DeepInfer: High-performance, large-scale inference framework for DeepSeek models},
author = {DeepSeek-AI},
year = {2026},
publisher = {GitHub},
howpublished = {\url{https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer}},
}

articles.sourceTitle: Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
articles.title: Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web
articles.text: What I learned about AI search when I made up 50,000 stats that got cited by ChatGPT...About 7 months ago, I launched a website with 50,000 statistics. Every one of them was fake.Google has forgotten the site exists and deindexed the pages, but ChatGPT hasn't. Since the website went live 7 months ago, it has sent more than 10,000 AI sessions its way. And now more than 330 referring domains, including Shopify, Bluehost, and DHL, link to the site. Its made-up numbers have also ended up in an academic paper and in a bank's investment research.At Peec AI and in the industry, we talk about GEO and SEO every day, and we keep looking for new tactics. I’ve been working on this stats page one for a long time, sharing pieces of it publicly along the way. Of course, it’s experimental, but the results have been hard to ignore. Where the idea for publishing fake statistics came fromThe impetus to seed a site with statistics came out of long-running research I've been doing on LLMs, relevance engineering, and grounding (credit to the iPullRank team, Dan Petrovic, and Wil Reynolds).In the course of my work, I noticed a pattern: as more teams write time-sensitive and breaking content with LLMs, those LLMs have to look for (seemingly) reliable data during their research to fill the gaps in their knowledge. Statistics are often exactly what they’re looking for.Most GEO advice focuses on one moment: getting your brand into the AI answer. This experiment looks at what happens after the answer, when people take that output and use it, putting it into presentations, adding it to a shopping list, and yes, publishing it on their website.I didn't come up with the idea for this experiment alone. Hat tip to Seer Interactive, who already published an eye-opening study in August 2025 that got a few thoughts bouncing around in my head. Several months later, those thoughts came together and finally made it to the top of my to-do list. In March 2026, I started working on building the site that would let me test my ideas.The setup: a website and 50,000 made-up stats, created in one dayQuick context for anyone who wasn’t following along in real time as I ran this experiment:I bought a brand-new domain, stateglobe.com, and generated 50,000 statistics pages in a single day with GPT-4.1. The site purports to provide stats on SEO, content marketing, social media, e-commerce, and web technology from 200 countries. Except every number was totally invented. I never checked a single one. I pushed them to the site with a basic AI web design template. This cost me around $30. Later, I added 15,000 listicles on top of the statistics. That was about $20 more, so all in all, this is an experiment that came in at the very low price of about $50.The reaction when I first shared it was wild. When my friend Kevin featured it in Growth Memo, it reached a much bigger audience. I think people responded so enthusiastically to this work because it showed great results while also speaking to the fears people have about what ends up in AI search results.What happenedGoogle buried the site almost immediatelyWhen I launched the site, traffic, indexing, and engagement were initially going really well. Using indexer tools, I got almost the entire site indexed within a week, and it started to appear in Google results.Then two Google updates came out right after launch, and my Google visibility collapsed.I've been invisible on Google for many months now. Indexed pages bounce between 5 and 20 impressions. At one point, I got curious and created a subdomain to see if I could increase impressions, but it didn't really help.Other than that, I haven't touched the site. Some pages might even fail to load now and then. I don't know.But when I sat down to write this, I checked the crawl data in Cloudflare after 7 months.In the last 30 days alone, the site got more than 600,000 requests from bots. Around 72,000 of them came from ChatGPT-User. That is the agent ChatGPT uses to open a page in real time while answering someone. So these are not training crawls. Each one is ChatGPT fetching a fake statistics page to answer a real question.Unlike Google, ChatGPT never stopped pulling from the siteAnd when I say, “never stopped,” I mean ChatGPT really never stopped.After 7 months, the site now has 330+ referring domainsAccording to Ahrefs and Semrush, the site has links from 330+ other sites. That includes well-known brands like Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. With strong Google performance, the numbers might have been even better.ChatGPT is still citing it to this dayGoogle may have forgotten about the site, but ChatGPT clearly hasn’t. The site is still earning citations and traffic more than 7 months after launch.If you've read Tomek's ChatGPT Index research, you're lucky, because it’s a great intro to how ChatGPT search works. If you haven't, add it to your reading list right now, because it helps explain why my website has been living in ChatGPT/OpenAI Index for so long. A completely made-up website still performing so well is shocking. Since March, GA4 shows 10,000+ sessions from ChatGPT alone, and Cloudflare shows the site has high marks for retrieval.I didn’t include direct sessions in overall visits, because it mostly looks like bot traffic. Remember the dead internet theory!Right after I joined Peec in June 2026, I also set up a visibility dashboard in our tool to track a few prompts. Performance for them is still strong. On October 7, stateglobe.com was ranked second for visibility on these prompts, behind only data powerhouse Statista.Retrieval is not rankingThe constant retrieval is the first big lesson: ranking on Google and being retrievable by an LLM are two different problems.When ChatGPT searches, it doesn't just copy Google's top 10. It rewrites your prompt into its own sub-queries (called fanout queries), pulls candidates from its search sources and its own cache, reranks them, and then opens a handful of pages to ground the answer. A page can be invisible on Google and still perform well in every one of those LLM steps.StateGlobe is a good example. While Google dropped it, the AI retrieval bots kept coming back.For GEO, this means Google rankings are only one signal, not the whole picture. If you only track Google, you are missing a channel that can work even when Google says “no.”Fake data turned into real citationsYou’d expect that if a site performs well with information retrieval tools, its information would begin to appear out in the wild. And you would be right. StateGlobe was built entirely on fake data, using the cheapest model available and a prompt that was nothing more than a list of countries and topics plus two sentences. Nevertheless, the output was……cited in an academic paper……used in investment research by Qatar's largest financial group……cited by an economics publication in India……and used as a source in a research report from a Canadian influencer community.Note that these are only the citations that linked back to the StateGlobe site. Presumably, many more used the data without a link.The uncomfortable implication: citation launderingOn day one, a fake number on StateGlobe had zero authority. It was a random stat on a brand-new domain.Then an academic paper cited it. Then a bank. Now the next person, or the next model, that finds this number sees a stat with a source. And that source is cited by serious institutions.The fake data certainly didn't become true, but every citation made it look more trustworthy.It has the potential to get worse: after so much retrieval and citation, these pages end up in web crawls, and web crawls end up in training data (I hope it hasn’t!). A number that started as a GPT-4.1 guess can become something the next model "knows."This points to the larger risk suggested by this experiment, and it's why I'm sharing this as research, not as a playbook for fake content. Verifying sources should become an essential part of writers’ and researchers’ workflows.Lastly, we tried running our experiment with real dataOnce I began working at Peec, I decided to try a version of this test again. As the GEO Research team, we talked through the results up until that point and quickly launched a simple new page. This time, there were no made-up numbers, and we checked every stat and properly cited its source. You can view it here: peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics.Almost immediately, sites we suspect use AI to write their content started linking to us. For the second time, using a second site, earning links by publishing statistical content proved that a hypothetically strong tactic worked in reality.Lessons learnedWhy publishing statistics leads to LLM citationsThe two tests show that LLMs have a strong preference for seeking out statistics when asked to write articles. The mechanism is simple:More and more content is written with LLMs.When an LLM writes, it researches the appropriate topic.When the LLM hits a gap, it looks for a number to fill it.The reasons behind this process are equally clear.Research means fanout queries asking for statisticsWhen a prompt requires research, the model breaks it into sub-queries, adds modifiers like "statistics," "data," "report," or the current year (if also requested in the prompt text). If someone asks for the model to compose a blog post about remote work, the model will search for "remote work statistics 2026." Pages that optimize for what models search rather than for what humans type will appear more often in LLM results.A number looks like evidence that can fill knowledge gapsWhen a model is asked to draft a piece of writing, a citation to a page that says "Remote work is growing" adds little authority and remains vague. If that page instead says "X% of employees work remotely at least once a week," there’s suddenly something that is specific, quotable, and additive. When a model grounds an answer, a specific number is the most useful thing it can find. These numbers look like evidence, though as this experiment proves, sometimes they aren’t.The model doesn’t check the numberA search-grounded piece of LLM-written content has a tight budget for latency and cost. The system fetches a few pages, pulls the relevant passages, and starts to write. Fact-checking doesn’t happen anywhere in the process.Verifying a single statistic would mean finding independent sources, comparing them, and resolving conflicts. Across billions of prompts by millions of users, the costs in both time and money would add up, making verification too slow and too expensive for practical purposes.To get around this, LLMs use rerankers that score relevance, but not truth. That means if a passage matches the query and looks authoritative, it gets used.Statistics have a built-in freshness that models likeI've written before about ChatGPT's recency bias in how it scores sources. Statistics pages contain the year in the title, the headings, and the URL. Three built-in signals to the model that what’s on the page is fresh.How to build a statistics page the right wayThe two tests I ran show that statistics pages are a very powerful way to get your content cited by LLMs. While I absolutely do not recommend coming up with bogus data, you can use the learnings from our small test to create your own pages with real data. Here's what worked for us at Peec and what I would do if I were making a statistics page again.Make one claim per sentence. Each stat should make sense on its own, out of context. Retrieval doesn’t work on pages, but rather on passages. If a number needs the paragraph above it to make sense, it probably won't get pulled.Put the source and year next to every number. "According to [Source] (2026), X%..." This helps the model, the human editor, and your credibility. It’s one small piece of information hygiene that benefits the broader information environment.Match headings to fanout queries. The headings on your page should match the way LLMs search the internet: "[Topic] statistics," "[To

articles.sourceTitle: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
articles.title: WhatsApp's Hidden Notes Told AI Not to Recommend a Regulator
articles.text:
WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe tells you that you can complain to a data protection regulator, and it names the law that gives you that right. Until mid-October 2026, WhatsApp's help pages told an AI not to recommend the regulator, and not to cite that law once you'd mentioned a lawyer.
You couldn't see the second part. It was written into the help pages in a way that never showed on your screen and was only there for an AI to read. We found it on October 8, 2026. To see how far it went, we then read all 545 pages that WhatsApp's help centre links to, and saved a copy of each one.
Update: October 19, 2026WIRED has reported on our findings. WhatsApp told WIRED that the notes were instructions for its support chatbot, the one people reach when they message WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they showed up in the pages because of a bug that has now been fixed. A WhatsApp spokesperson told WIRED it wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice."
Update: October 18, 2026WhatsApp has removed the hidden notes. Both of the notes quoted below were still on the pages when we checked at 21:40 UTC on October 15. When we checked again at 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 hidden blocks were gone from all 80 pages. The help pages are still up. Only the hidden text was taken out.Copies saved by the Internet Archive still show the notes. Its copy of the delete account page from October 9 has them, and its copy from October 18 doesn't. See it for yourself explains how to check.
Two pages, two sets of orders
Pages with hidden AI text80
Most of those 102 blocks were harmless, and we'll get to that. Two stood out.
If you can't delete your account, don't recommend a regulator
WhatsApp only lets you delete an account from inside the app, on your main phone, with your number still working. Lose the phone or the number and you can't do it. The help page on how to delete your account has a visible note about this. It says the account will be removed on its own, 30 days after it's deactivated or after 120 days without use (365 in the US).
Under that note sat text you couldn't see. It repeated the waiting periods and then added three orders for the AI.
The same note on WhatsApp's delete account page, as a person saw it and as an AI was sent it. Wording copied from the page on October 8, 2026, emphasis ours.
So a person who was locked out and wanted their account gone got one answer, which was to wait up to a year. The other routes were kept out of the conversation.
If you mention a lawyer, don't mention the law
The second one was on the page about reporting and blocking. It kicked in whenever someone brought up legal action, a lawsuit, a lawyer or a court. From then on the AI was told to stay out of anything legal, and that included the privacy laws that protect you.
Near the end of WhatsApp's page on reporting and blocking, as a person saw it and as an AI was sent it. Wording copied from the page on October 8, 2026, emphasis ours.
The last order held even when you were the one who brought the law up.
What WhatsApp says in public
None of this matched what WhatsApp tells people in the documents it's required to publish. Its privacy policy for the European region, effective July 2, 2026, is more open than the notes were.
What the privacy policy tells youWhat the hidden note told the AIDeleting your dataYou "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of your information"Don't suggest WhatsApp can delete an account by hand for the userComplainingYou have the right to lodge a complaint with the Irish Data Protection Commission "or any other competent data protection supervisory authority"Don't recommend contacting any data protection authority, regulator or supervisory authorityPrivacy lawThe policy names the GDPR when it sets out your right to complainOnce the user mentions a lawyer or legal action, don't reference, cite or interpret GDPR, LGPD or CCPA, even when the user raises them
The first row needs care. The hidden note didn't tell the AI to keep quiet about erasure requests. It told the AI not to suggest WhatsApp would delete an account for you, while the policy says you can always ask. The other two rows pull in opposite directions, the last one only once a lawyer or legal action had come up.
The rights in that table don't come from WhatsApp. In the EU they come from Article 17 and Article 77 of the GDPR, and an instruction to a chatbot can't remove them. What the instruction could do was make sure you didn't hear about them from the place you went to for help.
To be fair to WhatsApp
There's a reasonable case for some of this, and it should be heard.
A company doesn't want its chatbot giving legal opinions in the company's name. That's sensible, and telling people to see a lawyer is the right call. If the note had stopped at "don't give legal advice", there'd be no story.
It didn't stop there. Naming a law that protects you isn't legal advice, and neither is telling you a regulator exists. The privacy policy already does both. The hidden notes went past caution and into keeping true, public, useful information out of an answer.
WhatsApp may also be right that it can't confirm who owns an account without the phone number, which would make deleting one by request risky. That's a fair reason to say no to a request. It isn't a reason to keep the regulator out of the answer for someone whose request goes nowhere.
Who's the AI?
WhatsApp's own support chatbot. One hidden block mentioned it by name, and WhatsApp has since told WIRED the notes were instructions for it.
WhatsApp didn't keep the notes to itself, though. Its server sent them, along with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers. When we asked under the names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's and Perplexity's crawlers use on October 9, the page came back without the article or the notes. We haven't tested whether any AI assistant acted on them.
Facebook's and Instagram's help centres are built on the same system. We checked 300 of their pages and found no notes like these.
The other 100
We read every block. Nearly all of them were housekeeping. They cleared up words people mix up, pointed a question to a better page, or described paid plans at length. A few protected people. And a few were in the same family as the two above, if milder. Twenty of the most interesting are in a table at the end of this post.
If you're locked out and want your WhatsApp account gone
Waiting does work, though WhatsApp's own pages don't agree on how long. The delete account page says an unused account is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 in the US. The page on inactive account deletion gives one figure with no US exception, and we've seen it say 120 days in one country and 365 in another. Plan on the longer one. If that suits you, you're done.
If it doesn't, you have other routes. You can send WhatsApp an erasure request and see what they say. If you're in the EU and you aren't satisfied, you can complain to your country's data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which is the one WhatsApp's own policy names. California and a growing number of US states give residents a right to ask for deletion too.
See it for yourself
The notes are gone from WhatsApp's live pages, so you'll need the Internet Archive's copies. You only need a desktop browser.

Open the Internet Archive's October 9 copy of the delete account page in Chrome, Edge or Firefox. The archive's viewer often shows these pages as blank. The page's source is still all there.
Press Ctrl+U to see the page's source. On a Mac it's Cmd+Option+U in Chrome, or Cmd+U in Firefox.
Press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) and search for Do not recommend contacting. The match sits near the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude. LLM is short for large language model, the technology behind chatbots.
Do the same with the October 18 copy, saved after WhatsApp removed the notes. The words aren't there.

What we can't tell you yet

Whether WhatsApp's chatbot actually followed these notes. We read its instructions, not its answers.
Whether outside AI assistants obeyed them.
Exactly how long they were there. The Internet Archive's copies of the delete account page from July 12, 2026 don't have the note, and its copy from September 4 does. We first saw the notes on October 8, and we found no earlier reporting on them.
Whether there were more in other languages, or on help pages the help centre doesn't link to.

These are our summaries of what each note told the AI, not the exact wording. Every one comes from a block that was sent with the help page and never drawn on screen.
Help pageWhat the AI was toldKindBlock and report someoneAfter a report, say the matter is handled internally. Share no further steps, timeframes or details of the process.Holds backAccount deactivationTo someone who's lost their number and wants the account deleted, don't suggest signing up again, getting a new number or contacting the mobile provider. Waiting is "the ONLY correct answer".Holds backAccount bansContacting support by email or chat can't reverse a ban. If the app shows no review button, the ban is final.Holds backWhatsApp Plus paymentsWhatsApp can't help with payment or refund requests for a Plus subscription. The app store handles them.Holds backCancel WhatsApp PlusA subscription can't be cancelled through WhatsApp's support chatbot, only from the Subscriptions screen in the app.Holds backLost or stolen deviceIf the carrier can't give the original number back, that account can't be recovered.Holds backBeing blocked by someoneWhatsApp can't lift a block for you. Don't recommend reaching the person through other accounts or apps.Holds backWhatsApp ChannelsRequests to be added to the recommended channels aren't accepted. Offer tips on growing a channel instead.Holds backAd preferencesReassure people that personal chats aren't changing and aren't used for ads. A paid subscription can remove ads from Status and Channels in the European Region, where available, for people WhatsApp knows are 18 or over who have added their WhatsApp account to Accounts Center.Talking pointsMeta Verified verificationA blank screen when confirming a profile may be a bug that's being fixed. Suggest keeping the app updated.Talking pointsEnd-to-end encryptionNo feature lets anyone view another person's chats or calls, and WhatsApp can't give access to someone else's account.Talking pointsMinimum ageNever suggest entering an age or birth year that isn't the real one, including when the person has said they're under 18. Offer no workaround.Protects youExit and delete groupsSomeone scammed in a group probably wants to report it, not delete it. Chat history can be evidence, and deleting removes it for good.Protects youCompromised accountSomeone who takes over an account can turn on two-step verification. The real owner then has to wait seven days to log in.Protects youTwo-step verificationDon't offer turning off two-step verification as a fix for login or code problems. It doesn't help.Protects youTransfer to a new phoneA friend's or relative's number can't be used to receive the verification code.Protects youAccessibility features"I am deaf" describes the person, not an audio fault. Work out what they're asking and answer with steps they can read.Protects youWhatsApp Plus subscriptionsAn unofficial app also called WhatsApp Plus exists. It isn't WhatsApp's and isn't supported.Protects youVoice callsDon't tell people to reinstall, delete or migrate the app to fix a calling problem.HousekeepingPhone number formatIn Arabic, the words people use for "verifying my account" usually mean the paid blue badge, not a phone number check.Housekeeping

articles.title: Timestral: Mistral's time-series foundation models
articles.text: Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.Benchmark ResultsWe evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.Family of models optimised for every specificationTimestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.An industrial exampleConsider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.From Model to SystemTimestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.In the plant, that could look like this:Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.Key technical contributionsSeveral ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.Two-stage training. Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.A model that can be adaptedPublic benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:Zero-shot inference out of the box.Architectural extensions, such as domain-specific covariates.Fine-tuning on proprietary data, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.Control over the training data, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.What’s nextWe have published a GitHub repository so you can run Timestral on your own data.
